lines: You may fish for it, but every one you catch must go back into the water, quickly and carefully. You can't keep any.
In the book’s words
Catch and Release: You may fish for the named species, but you must release any that you catch.
Rule book p.4 ↗
gl:catch_and_release.title: Catch and release (release)

lines: An add-on to your basic licence that pays for conservation; you need one only for what it names: Kootenay Lake rainbow trout, Shuswap Lake char, Shuswap rainbow trout, salmon, Steelhead. Keeping some of these fish also means recording them on your licence right away.
In the book’s words
Your basic angling licence can be validated with up to five annual Conservation Surcharge Stamps, plus a White Sturgeon Conservation Licence.
Rule book p.5 ↗ p.7 ↗
gl:conservation_surcharge.title: Conservation Surcharge Stamp

lines: Only an artificial fly on the line (one single-pointed hook) — no bait or lure, no float or strike indicator, no sinker or split shot, no spinner or other attracting device. Where a water is fly fishing only, that is the only way to fish it.
In the book’s words

fly fishing: angling with a line to which only an artificial fly is attached (floats, sinkers, or attracting devices may not be attached to the line when fishing is restricted to "fly fishing only"). artificial fly: a single-pointed hook that is dressed only with fur, feathers, hair, textiles, tinsel and/or wire, and to which no external weight or external attracting device is attached. Two or more hooks tied in tandem is not permitted. Where gear is restricted to artificial flies, floats and sinkers may be attached to the line. Where areas are restricted to "fly fish only" floats and sinkers may not be attached to the line or fly.
Rule book p.80 ↗
gl:fly_fishing.title: Fly fishing only

lines: You may not fish for it at all, not even to release it. If you catch one by accident, release it at once.
In the book’s words

No fishing for: you may not deliberately fish for the species named even if your intention is to release any fish that you may catch. If you accidentally catch a fish of the species named, you must release it as quickly and carefully as possible.
Rule book p.4 ↗
gl:no_fishing_for.title: No fishing for (closed)

lines: A hook with one point (no treble) and no barb — you may pinch the barb flat. Every river, stream, creek and slough in B.C. requires it; on a lake only where its row says so.
In the book’s words

barbless hook: a hook without a barb on any part of the hook, including both the point and shank. Existing tackle may be modified by completely removing the barb, or by crimping the barb down so that its point is flush against the shaft. single hook: a hook having only one point. (In contrast, a treble hook is a hook having three points on a common shaft.) Note: use of a treble hook is permitted unless "single hook" is specified. It is unlawful to use barbed hooks or a hook with more than one point in any river, stream, creek or slough in B.C. (Note: the use of barbed hooks in lakes is permitted, unless noted in the Regional Water-Specific Tables).
Rule book p.8 ↗ p.80 ↗
gl:single_barbless_hook.title: Single barbless hook

lines: A rainbow trout that went to sea and came back: on waters where they run, any rainbow over 50 cm is a steelhead and follows the steelhead rules. Every wild steelhead must be released; you may keep at most 10 hatchery steelhead a licence year in all of B.C.
In the book’s words

steelhead: a rainbow trout longer than 50 cm in waters where anadromous rainbow trout are found. Both hatchery and wild steelhead may be found in B.C. waters. The annual province-wide quota for hatchery steelhead is 10. All wild steelhead must be released. Your basic licence must be validated with a Conservation Surcharge Stamp if you fish for steelhead anywhere in B.C. (whether you keep or release your catch). You must immediately record your retention of hatchery steelhead on your basic angling licence.
Rule book p.6 ↗ p.80 ↗
gl:steelhead.title: Steelhead

lines: A Steelhead Conservation Surcharge Stamp, added to your basic licence. You need it to fish for steelhead anywhere in B.C., even if you release them — and on many Classified Waters, on set dates, whatever you fish for. $28.57 a year for B.C. residents, $68.57 for everyone else.
In the book’s words

The annual province-wide quota for hatchery steelhead is 10. All wild steelhead must be released. Your basic licence must be validated with a Conservation Surcharge Stamp if you fish for steelhead anywhere in B.C. (whether you keep or release your catch). You must immediately record your retention of hatchery steelhead on your basic angling licence.
Rule book p.5 ↗ p.6 ↗ p.7 ↗
gl:steelhead_stamp.title: Steelhead Stamp

lines: B.C. residents under 16 need no licence or stamp and have their own quota. Under-16s from elsewhere need no licence either, but must fish with someone 16 or older who holds the licences and stamps the fishing needs — and what they keep counts toward that person's quota. To have their own quota, they buy the licences a 16+ angler would.
In the book’s words

If you are under 16 and NOT a resident of B.C.: You do not require any licence or stamp, but you must be accompanied by a person 16 years or older who holds the appropriate licences and stamps. Any fish you keep must be counted as part of the catch and possession of your accompanying licence holder.
Rule book p.6 ↗
gl:under_16.title: Anglers under 16

lines: Wild · adipose fin there
Hatchery · clipped, a healed scar instead
Look on the back, just in front of the tail. A small fin there means wild. Only a scar means hatchery. If you can’t tell, treat the fish as wild.
Hatchery or wild (adipose fin)

Hatchery trout and steelhead are marked before release by removing the adipose fin — the small fleshy fin on the back between the dorsal fin and the tail — so a hatchery fish has a healed scar there. A fish with its adipose fin (or a fresh, unhealed wound) is wild. Where only hatchery fish may be kept, every wild one goes back.
In the book’s words

hatchery trout: in some waters, hatchery trout may be harvested but wild trout must be released. In these waters, hatchery trout are marked before stocking by removal of their adipose fin. Therefore, these hatchery trout must have a healed scar in place of the missing fin. wild trout: in some waters, hatchery trout may be harvested but wild trout must be released. In these waters, wild trout will not be marked as hatchery fish and will have a normal adipose fin, or will have an unhealed scar in place of that fin, if missing.
Rule book p.13 ↗ p.80 ↗
hatch.title: Hatchery or wild?

lines: Possession: 2 days’ quota. Fish at home don’t count.
The fish you have with you at any time — in camp, a cooler or a vehicle.
For example:
With 4 trout and char a day you may have 8: 2 days’ fish. Possession doubles the 4 a day, not the 2 from streams.
With 15 whitefish a day you may have 30: 2 days’ fish.
With 20 bass a day you may have 40: 2 days’ fish.
In the rule book’s words

possession quota: the number of fish of any species that an angler may have in their possession at any given time, EXCEPT at place of ordinary residence. In most instances, the possession quota is two times the daily quota. See Tables for exceptions.

lines: Black crappie · Duane Raver / USFWS (fws.gov)

Deep, flat body covered in black speckles
Large, rounded back and bottom fins
Mouth reaches the front of the eye
sp:BCB.title: Black crappie

lines: Coastal cutthroat trout · Freshwater Fisheries Society of BC (GoFishBC)
Westslope cutthroat trout · Freshwater Fisheries Society of BC (GoFishBC)
What to look for
Red or orange slash under the lower jaw (may be faint)
Large mouth, reaching well past the eye
Black spots all over, more toward the tail
sp:CT.title: Cutthroat trout

lines: Bull trout · Joel Sartore / National Geographic (Commons)
Dolly Varden · WDFW (eRegulations WA)
What to look for
Pale pink or cream spots, smaller than the pupil
No worm-like markings on the back fin
White front edges on the lower fins
Bull trout: big, broad, flat head
sp:DV.title: Dolly Varden/bull trout

lines: Brook trout · Freshwater Fisheries Society of BC (GoFishBC)
What to look for
Worm-like markings on the back and back fin
Red spots with blue halos
Orange lower fins with white front edges
sp:EB.title: Brook trout

lines: Brown trout · Duane Raver / USFWS (fws.gov)
What to look for
Black and red spots, many with pale halos
Tail with few or no spots
Orange-rimmed adipose fin
sp:GB.title: Brown trout

lines: Kokanee · spawning · WDFW (sockeye male) (eRegulations WA)
Kokanee · Freshwater Fisheries Society of BC (GoFishBC)
What to look for
No black spots on the sides
Dark blue back, bright silver sides
Long fin under the tail end (13 or more rays)
sp:KO.title: Kokanee

lines: Largemouth bass · Duane Raver / USFWS (Commons)
What to look for
Dark stripe along the side
Jaw reaches past the back of the eye
Front and back fins almost separate
sp:LMB.title: Largemouth bass

lines: Lake trout · Sherman F. Denton (Commons)
What to look for
Pale spots all over a dark body, no red
Worm-like light markings on the back and back fin
Deeply forked tail
sp:LT.title: Lake trout

lines: Lake whitefish · Sherman F. Denton (Commons)
What to look for
Large scales, silver sides
Small mouth under a blunt snout
Has an adipose fin; no spots
sp:LW.title: Lake whitefish

lines: Rainbow trout · Freshwater Fisheries Society of BC (GoFishBC)
What to look for
Pink or red band along the side
Small black spots, mostly above the middle of the side
Rows of black spots on the tail
sp:RB.title: Rainbow trout

lines: Steelhead · ocean · Freshwater Fisheries Society of BC (GoFishBC)
Steelhead · spawning · WDFW (eRegulations WA)

A rainbow trout that went to sea: bright silver
Faint spots, mostly on the back and tail
Hatchery steelhead are missing this small fin (the adipose fin)

lines: White sturgeon · Joseph Huët (Paris Museum) (Commons)
What to look for
Rows of bony plates, no scales
Barbels under a pointed snout
Upper lobe of the tail much longer
